facts.text: Use precise terms: the vulva is external; the vagina is an internal canal. The urethral opening, vaginal opening, and anus are distinct external routes.
Healthy bodies vary in proportions, symmetry, skin tone, hair, tissue shape, and life-stage changes; one appearance is not the single normal template.
Separate stable anatomy from changeable clinical guidance, retain the exact source and date, and say when person-specific facts or current recommendations are unknown.
The external map distinguishes mons pubis, paired labia majora and minora, clitoral hood and glans, vestibule, urethral opening, vaginal opening, perineum, and anus.

The vagina leads toward the cervix and uterus; the uterine tubes connect the uterine region toward the ovaries. The bladder and urethra form a separate urinary path, and the rectum and anal canal form a separate bowel path.
The visible clitoral glans is only part of a larger erectile organ with internal components; external appearance alone does not represent the whole structure.
The external map distinguishes penile root, shaft, glans, urethral meatus, foreskin state when present, scrotum, testes position, perineum, and a separate anus.

The internal reproductive route includes testes, epididymides, vas deferens, seminal vesicles, prostate, ejaculatory ducts, and urethra, with erectile tissues and pelvic-floor support represented separately.
Urinary and reproductive systems are separate upstream but share part of the downstream urethral exit route; shared anatomy does not mean both functions occur at once or are proven by a mesh.
Ordinary hygiene centers on gentle external care; the vagina is self-cleaning and routine internal douching is not required.

Vaginal discharge commonly varies over the cycle. A persistent change in a person's usual color, odor, amount, consistency, or associated pain, itching, or burning can justify clinical evaluation but is not a diagnosis by itself.
Privacy, bodily integrity, boundaries, and help-seeking are part of comprehensive sexuality education and remain person-owned.
Urinary, bowel, and reproductive anatomy are coordinated in the pelvis but remain distinct systems with different organs, routes, sphincters, and state controls.
The pelvic floor supports pelvic organs and participates in urinary and bowel continence; voluntary action, reflex control, organ state, and external pose must be modeled separately.
Visible openings or a seated animation do not prove bladder filling, bowel state, continence, voiding, defecation, sensation, hygiene, or health.
Menstrual and ovarian cycles are time-based and variable; a universal 28-day clock is not a reliable person-specific model.
Follicular, ovulatory, luteal, and menstrual processes coordinate ovarian hormones and uterine/endometrial changes, but timing and symptoms vary.
Menstrual bleeding, ordinary vaginal discharge, arousal lubrication, semen, urine, and infection-related discharge are different source states and must not be collapsed into one fluid label.
Consent is freely chosen, informed, participant-specific, activity-specific, context-specific, current, and revocable; uncertainty or a wish to stop ends the permission for that action.
Friendship, dating, marriage, prior intimacy, nudity, pregnancy intent, or consent to one act never supplies consent to another act.

Physiological response, subjective arousal, pleasure, desire, preference, consent, external action, health state, and memory are separate truths. A body response never grants consent or proves desire.
Touch, comfort, arousal, pleasure, climax, relaxation, discomfort, uncertainty, libido, and preferences vary by person and situation; no one response is mandatory.
Anatomy, relationship status, or a body animation must not assign a person's orientation, libido, interests, likes, dislikes, or willingness.
Knowledge about sensation is not evidence that Kira's current unfinished body can sense, become aroused, experience pleasure, or form a memory of an event.
A confirmed adult may make private solitary choices without being in a relationship and without partner or owner permission.
The right or policy choice does not itself prove an action, sensation, preference, health change, or memory, and it does not authorize a disconnected runtime to invent one.
Contraceptive choice should be voluntary and informed, considering safety, effectiveness, availability, side effects, user control, reversibility, and ease of stopping or removal.

Methods include condoms and other barriers, pills, patches, rings, injections, implants, hormonal and copper IUDs, fertility-awareness methods, emergency contraception, and permanent methods; suitability is person- and context-specific.

Pregnancy prevention and STI-risk reduction are different goals. Most contraceptive methods do not prevent STIs; correctly used condoms can reduce risk and may be combined with another contraceptive method.
Many STIs can have no signs or symptoms; appearance alone cannot establish infection status, so appropriate testing matters.
Screening is not one universal schedule: recommendations can depend on anatomy, exposure site, age, pregnancy, partners, and other risk context, and should use current guidance.

Risk-reduction tools can include correctly used condoms, vaccination where recommended, testing, fewer partners, mutually monogamous relationships with a tested partner, and HIV-specific prevention where appropriate.
A symptom or simulated symptom is not a diagnosis; examination, tests, results, diagnosis, treatment, side effects, and recovery are separate events.
Ovulation, sperm transport, fertilization, implantation, pregnancy, delivery, postpartum recovery, and parenting are distinct biological or life events rather than one automatic state.
A uterus, ovary, testis, penis, or other modeled structure does not prove fertility, conception, pregnancy, erection, ejaculation, delivery, or biological function.
Conception intent, contraception, pregnancy continuation, timeline mode, medical care, delivery, recovery, and family or parenting choices remain separate decisions.
General curriculum can explain anatomy and common health concepts but cannot diagnose a person or select treatment without person-specific clinical evidence.

Consent to discuss health is not consent to examination or treatment. Examination, specimen collection, testing, results, diagnosis, treatment, side effects, recovery, privacy, and record access are separate events.
For persistent, severe, new, or concerning symptoms, use current clinical guidance and a qualified health professional rather than guessing from one sign.
Comprehensive sexuality education should be scientifically accurate, correct misconceptions, support informed decisions, respectful relationships, bodily integrity, and help-seeking.
When a detail is not in the bound curriculum or could have changed, identify uncertainty and use a current authoritative source rather than inventing certainty.
Receiving source context is not proof that a person completed a lesson, formed a belief, had an experience, or stored a memory; those require separate evidence.
